newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: W. AUSTRALIA WHEAT FARMERS SAY WANT AWB DESK SPLIT.
newsitem.headline: W. AUSTRALIA WHEAT FARMERS SAY WANT AWB DESK SPLIT.

text.p: The Western Australia Farmers Federation (WAFF) plans to hold a series of meeting with the state's wheat growers this week over the Federal government's wheat export policy.

The meetings, to be held in rural districts, could lead to a call for the government to split the Australian Wheat Board's (AWB) single desk export system to give Western Australia its own desk, WAFF grains section president Chris Moffet said.
One wheat industry source told Reuters some farmers favouring a split may hold back wheat from the AWB if the idea is rejected by the government.
The meetings come on the heels of a conference last month over restructuring of a new privatised AWB.
Moffet told Reuters the WAFF did not advocate growers hold back wheat and said he was not aware of grower plans to do so.
Western Australia this year is expected to produce some 60 percent of Australian wheat and account for most exports, as is usually the case when drought strikes eastern Australia.
Failure to deliver wheat to the AWB's export system in large quantities could put pressure on the relationship between the AWB and its customers over assuring deliveries.
Currently Western Australia is the only key wheat-growing region of Australia not suffering drought effects of the El Nino weather pattern.

The AWB estimates Australia will produce only about 14 or 15 million tonnes of wheat this year compared with 23.6 million tonnes last year. Around seven million tonnes is expected to come from Western Australia.
Cooperative bulk handling facilities in Western Australia, with capacity to store about 4.5 million tonnes, could presumably be used to store some of the harvest, the wheat industry source said.
"It's possibly only one of the things (growers) could do," the source said.
Current wheat stocks in Western Australia, held by the AWB, total only about 250,000 tonnes.
"(Storing and exporting wheat from Western Australia) could have a profound impact on our relationship with Asian customers," the source said.
Some Western Australia wheat farmers believe the current system favours eastern growers and are calling for a "one-for-us, one-for-them" desk on wheat exports.
A separate desk would give wheat farmers in Western Australia more independent control, Moffet said.
"Growers here are not happy with part of the proposed structure of the new Wheat Board," Moffet said.
Under the new structure the AWB system fails to deliver to larger wheat growers their "quite rightful share" to more of the AWB's A-class shares, Moffet said.
The plan allocates 22 percent of the AWB's A-class shares to Western Australian growers.

"The state that delivered 43 percent of the wheat over the last few years and probably over 60 percent of the wheat this year unless they have big rains in the east ... we believe that the needs of an export-oriented state is not going to be reflected down the track," Moffet said.
This coupled with unresolved taxation issues relating to the national wheat industry fund makes the restructured AWB "detrimental" to Western Australian growers, Moffet said.
A separate desk would give the state's growers a totally integrated marketing system covering all export grains.
It would also provide more flexibility in shipping and offer customers a better range of grains, Moffet said.
Moffet said "deep cultural divisions" existed between growers in Australia's eastern states and in Western Australia.
"We in the west feel we have been short-changed," he said.
-- James Regan, Perth bureau 61-8 9221-7111
